props.title: Les Mistons

sections.content: François Truffaut's **Les Mistons** (1957) marks a pivotal moment in French New Wave cinema, arriving just before his revolutionary The 400 Blows (1959). This 18-minute short follows five mischievous boys who torment a young couple, capturing both childhood cruelty and innocence through innovative handheld camerawork and natural performances. The film establishes Truffaut's signature themes of youth, desire, and observation that would define his later masterpieces like **Jules and Jim** (1962) and **Day for Night** (1973).

sections.content: The DNA of **Les Mistons** runs through countless coming-of-age films that followed. Its influence is visible in works like **My Life as a Dog** (1985), where young protagonists navigate the complexities of adult relationships through a lens of childhood confusion. Maurice Pialat's **L'Enfance Nue** (1968) adopts similar documentary-like observations of youth, while **The Spirit of the Beehive** (1973) echoes Les Mistons' exploration of children processing adult mysteries. SUBHEAD: The French New Wave Connection

As one of Truffaut's earliest works, **Les Mistons** demonstrates the emerging stylistic hallmarks of the French New Wave - location shooting, jump cuts, and direct camera address. These techniques would be expanded in contemporaneous works like Jean-Luc Godard's **Breathless** (1960) and Agnès Varda's **La Pointe Courte** (1955). The film's treatment of voyeurism and youth anticipates later New Wave classics like Jacques Rozier's **Adieu Philippine** (1962).
